newsitem.title: BOSNIA: International powers halt Bosnia refugee returns.
newsitem.headline: International powers halt Bosnia refugee returns.

text.p: International powers implementing the peace accord in Bosnia have suspended a refugee return process until a crisis caused by communal violence in the northeast was resolved, a Western official said on Wednesday.

Colum Murphy, spokesman for the office of the High Representative in Bosnia, said the country's national leaders were told on Tuesday in a letter that the procedure was on hold until certain demands were met and calm returned to the region.
About 600 Moslems, some armed, entered the village of Gajevi on Monday in the de-militarised Zone of Separation (ZOS) between Serb and government-held territory in the northeast.

But refugees who remained in the village during the night fled after an early morning battle on Tuesday involving gunfire and grenades on both sides. One Moslem was killed and two Serbs and two Moslems were injured.
The letter suspending the programme of refugee returns was signed by NATO, the U.N.'s aid agency and police and the Office of the High Representative Carl Bildt.

In the letter, they demanded that all Moslems return to Moslem-Croat territory, that the ban on weapons in the ZOS be respected and that all sides end any action that could inflame the situation, Murphy said.

An international commission was established in October to examine applications from refugees wanting to return to their homes across the ethnic fault-lines, after conflict errupted when Moslems occupied several villages in Serb territory.
So far, the returns have been limited to villages inside the Zone of Separation.

"Until we are satisfied that our demands are fulfilled and the situation has calmed down, the procedure for returns is suspended for the entire Zone of Separation with immediate effect," Murphy told reporters in Sarajevo.
"The international commission will neither receive nor process any new or old applications."
Under the Dayton peace accord, refugees were granted an unrestricted right to return to their homes, but aid officials say hostile Serb authorities have made the programme all but impossible.
Tension around Gajevi remained high on Wednesday, when some 500 Moslems marched to a NATO checkpoint blocking their way into the town, and threatened to bypass the peacekeepers.
NATO spokesman Major Brett Boudreau condemned the Moslem's demonstration as provocative.
"It violated the intent of Dayton, which provides for orderly, peacefull and phased returns," NATO spokesman Major Brett Boudreau said.
In the incident that sparked Tuesday's conflict, Boudreau said Moslems on Monday organised a large group of armed people who proceeded through the Zone of Separation without approval.
A U.N. Police Task Force spokesman said NATO and the U.N. on Monday also tried to negotiate a joint search of Gajevi village with Serb police, but failed to reach an agreement.
Nevertheless, about 50 armed Serb police went ahead with their search early on Tuesday, the spokesman Alex Ivanko said.
